blocks.x: This is Edmund Hall, and I'd like to thank Harry Susha and Dick Allen for the wonderful tribute they paid to me a few days ago on this jazz program. And also I want to thank all the fans also.
Okay, anytime you're ready.

This is Edmund Hall. I would like to thank Harry Susha, the president of the New Orleans Jazz Club, and Dick Allen for the wonderful tribute they paid to me a few days ago. And I want to thank also all the jazz fans. I think we got the thing going.
Anybody can start talking all the time you're out there.
Alright, want me to ask him some questions? Yeah, sure. Alright. The first thing we'll start at the beginning, might as well. Where were you born?

I was born in what's called Reserve Louisiana. Reserve Louisiana? Yeah, Reserve Louisiana. It's about what, about 20, 21 to 22 miles from here. And what date was that? That was May the 15th, 1901. Were any of your family musicals? Oh yeah, everybody's musical, whole musical family. My father was a kind of player. He used to play with the famous Onward band here. I guess you might have read the story away. He also was, he went to New York with the band. I think it was 18, we had a little discussion about that. Some people say it was 1896. I found out this morning it was 1892. 1892. 1892. 1892. The Onward band. Yeah, this one was the Onward band and Jim Umfress was the leader of the band. Willie Umfress's father.
Grandfather, I think. Yeah, that's right. Young Willie. Now, could he read?
I think so. Yeah, the whole band used to read, yeah. Yeah. The Onward band, I know all the members.
How did you get started in music? Did he help you?

Well, yeah, quite after he got a certain age, he had all these kinds, you know, years ago that a clarinet player in a band had two or three different kinds of guys, A clarinet, B flat, C, A flat, so he had all of them. So quite nice, he just had five boys in the band, I mean five boys in the family. So he just passed out clarinet, you know what I mean? He had all his clarinet, everybody just picked up a clarinet, started playing. I also had an uncle who was a guitar player, practically all the boys can play guitar too.
What was your uncle's name by the way?
Oh, his name was, I don't know, I don't even know his right name, his name was Chunk. Chunk. Yeah.
That was his nickname.
That was his nickname.
Then did he play around?
Well, no, just play for, just his own amusement, you know, no gigging around, just his own amusement.
What was your first instrument? Was it clarinet?

No, my first instrument was guitar. I used to work with Thomas playing guitar. Oh, I see, with guitar? Yeah, then later on I started to play with the clarinet. My oldest brother was the same way, he started on guitar, then changed the clarinet, so I picked up the guitar and then I changed the clarinet too.
Did you have lessons on guitar?
No, I just picked it up.
I see. And your first, your very first job was with who?
My very first job, I think it was with Thomas Band, it's been so long ago, I think it was Thomas, just a bunch of kids, we picked up our instruments after playing.
Do you remember the names of the other fellows at all?

I think it was Thomas Valentine, the trumpet player. We had a drummer by the name of Lionel, I don't know what his last name is, man. The Creole name? No, I don't think so. Is he Lionel Thomas? I can't think of his name.
It might be the fellow who's working with Billy and the Dee, Bill, what's his last name? I forget it.
He used to work with an old time band around Reserve by the name of Dejon.
I know Harold Dejon, huh?

Harold Dejon. He's a sax player, he must be young. No, but this Dejon, he had one son, but he died just some time ago. I don't think he was a musician either. He's a sax player. Probably a relative, something like that.

There is a Lionel here playing drums, and his last name begins with a T, working out as much as Billy and the Dee Pierce. Could be, he was an old timer. He's an old timer, he's just starting back. He could look that good. Billy was a, what was Billy's maiden named Goodson, she's from Pensacola. Isn't that right, Bill? Yeah.
In Pensacola.
I don't know. There's a whole family of sisters over there, you might know. His brothers, they all play piano. Who else was in the band? Drums, trumpet, guitar? Drums, bass?

Oh yeah, I remember the bass player name, he died just not so very long. My sister was saying, his name was Cessin, bass player. Can I remember that far back? Lionel was playing drums, Cessin playing bass. I was playing, Thomas was playing trumpet. I was playing the guitar. Did we have a trumpet? I can't think of the trombone player's name. We had a trombone too, but I can't play a song. I know the trombone player, I can't think of his name. Did he come to the city?
No.
I think he did come here, but later on. I can't think of his name.
What happened after you, in music after that?

Well what happened after music after, then I came to New Orleans and I joined the Bud Roussel band. I remember the first job I played with Lee Collin. Lee Collin was the first guy I worked with here. Bud Roussel, played a place back at the, it was a station up on Ramport Street, and I was a place back there used to be called the Function. I remember one Saturday night I got a job playing with Bud Roussel and Lee Collin, who happened to be playing trumpet in that band. Did you work regularly with him? Yeah, I worked with him for quite a while. Then there was another band I got with by the name of Gus Matkatt, a trombone player, used to live uptown. You ever heard of him? That's news to me. Gus Matkatt, a trombone player. Gus Matkatt, a trombone player. Came in the kid over and could play as her brother.
Who was in Bud Roussel's band? Do you remember other than Lee?
Lee Collin, Bud Roussel, bass. All I can remember, I remember the drummer, his name was Happy.
Was that Red Happy?
No, I think you had a Red Happy and a Black Happy, was it? Well it was Black Happy.

That's Christopher Billston, he's still alive. He's still alive, yeah. I saw him Mardi Gras day, he was playing a parade for the Zillow. He's still alive. You saw him building. Yeah, I saw him. And who else was, do you remember any of the other fellas?
No, I don't remember any of the other guys was in the band.
What about Buddy Petit, when you started working with him?

Well Buddy Petit, that, I don't know how I happened to get in that band. I'm trying to think, I'm trying to untangle this story. How did I happen to get with Buddy Petit? But I remember, frankly, all the guys in Buddy Petit's band. Cause we left, after I got with the band, then we left and went to Covington, Louisiana. That was about 1920 when that picture was taken. Cause I remember that was taken out in the street in Covington, Louisiana.
Who was in Gus Metcalf? I was wondering about that.

Well I tell you, Gus Metcalf was a trauma one player. He was one of the kind of guys, when he'd get a gig like that, he'd go around and get different musicians, just pick up a band. Tonight you'd be playing with one bunch of guys, next night you, you know what I mean.
Do you remember any outstanding men that played with Gus? No. That's new to me. I just, I'd like to trace him down. I could, he might still be around.

Who else was in Buddy's band? Did you have the... Well Buddy, let's see, when I got with Buddy's band, he had this boy Buddy Manatee playing banjo, Chester Zardas, bass. Faiso was the drummer, George Washington, trombone. He was, we had now played on bass, trombone. Buddy was on.
Buddy Manatee. Buddy Manatee.
Was he with him? Yeah, Buddy Manatee was.
He was with him. That's it, that's the man. In the picture exactly the same. Were there any changes? Did anybody...
No, when I left him, that same one, but the singer there, I don't know who he was. I never remember his name.
I was wondering who some of your ideas were when you came here. Any man you patented your playing on, in particular?
Yeah, well I like, I used to like Jimmy Noon.
Mm-hmm.
Johnny Dot. That was when you first got here? When I first got here. Yeah.
Big Eil Louie.

He had your own style, didn't he? No, no, he was mentioning about the guy that was playing, you know. What was the guy who was working at the, working with, what's the name of this, Piku? Piku. Yeah, it was another fellow who used to work with Robichaud. Charlie McCurtis? No, no. One of them, Tio's. Tio, what's his name? Lorenzo.
Yeah. That's the one. We just played some of his records yesterday.

Yeah. Tiro. Because I remember when Robichaud was going to New York, he was, Maison Blanche I think, is the one who financed the whole trip when they did their first recording and went to New York. Robichaud. Yeah, Robichaud with the band. Oh, Piron. Piron. Piron. Piron. He was a cripple guy. Used to play a left hand violin. Sure. And the last dance to give, I remember it was at the Knights of Pison Hall I think, somewhere up here on Ramport Street. And I happened to go to the dance.
What were some of Buddy Petit's tunes?
Boy, he played all of these tunes, all of these Dixon Van Tune, Heiser, the clarinet, Marmalade, Tin Roof Blues. Did he make up any numbers? Tin Roof Blues was Buddy's. Buddy made up Tin Roof Blues.
Well it had a special name then though.

Yeah. You wouldn't want to say that. It had a special name. Don't. None of it. And Tin Roof Blues was a background to a guy playing a solo. So the background was taking me the tune out of it. When I heard it, it was Tin Roof Blues. That was the new name for it.
Yeah. Now while I checked up on that name.
Well you know the name, Nigel.

Yeah, I know the name. I asked Punch at Eddie Barrett, and I said, we were playing a little job, and I asked him, let's play that number just to see if they would play it. Yeah. And they played it just right. So that's got to be the right name. I thought I'd double check. Did you go anywhere besides Covington?

Yeah, we went on a tour. After we closed in Covington, we went somewhere in Alabama, Mississippi. We toured for a while. And I think you mentioned a fella that had something to do with us after we left Covington, Louisiana. It's a Covington Hotel over there.
George Blanchett, is that the fella you found? I don't know.
I can't remember his name, but we had an agent, so I know that.
He used to hire Buddy. He said Buddy looked like a puff adder when he played. That's right. Yeah, he puffed out. His cheeks and his...
Was it one side, both sides? I think he did puffs out on both sides. Yeah.
Red apple, that's what I heard music he said.
And you couldn't miss him, you'd notice him if you'd see him on the street. You ever seen him in person?
Never did.

I never seen a guy, you'd had to notice him. He wore a brown derby, and he kind of, I think he was mixed with Indian. It had to be. His complexion and his hair, he had the hair, he looked like a horseman. I never seen a guy with the hair with such a coarse ring. Oh, just a poor face.
Just a poor face. It might have been Indian, you know, they've got that straight hair. A lot of, so many, mixed his hair. Yeah.
He wasn't very tall. No, no, just a regular size. He wasn't tall as I.
He looked short, actually.

Yeah, he looks short. By the way, you're talking about that tour, then we left and went to Galveston. We left and went to Galveston, Texas. We went to Houston, Texas. First we left here and went to Houston, Texas to play a job. And after we was in Houston for a while, then another guy came out to us and said he got a job for us to go to Galveston, Texas. So we went to Galveston, Texas. I'll never forget, we took a piano player from here with us, but after we got in, after we got out there in Texas, we found out this piano player wasn't what he's supposed to be, so we hired another piano player up there by the name of Lazy Daddy, and he played with us. And we was up there for about three or four months. Then we left there and came to Lake Charles, Louisiana, and played with a bunch there for a while. That's how we, but it split up. stuff
Buddy Petit came home, Faiso came home. So Tom won't play by the name of Ambrose, you might have heard of him.
He's Lawrence Tucker's uncle. I can't locate him. He had his last name.

Yeah, because they left me, I stayed with that band, they left me in Lake Charlton, Louisiana. I stayed with the band, but Buddy came back here. But after I came back here then we got together and that's how we happened to go to Florida, to Pensacola, Florida, got the band up together again, went to Pensacola, Florida.
What sort of piano did Lazy Daddy play?
Oh, he was one of them really good ones, at that particular time.
Did he have a special kind of bass or anything?
No, no, because he had been in the business for a long time because he was in Mexico playing for shows and singers and all that kind of stuff.
He came from out of Texas, that way?
Yeah, he came from somewhere in Texas, out that way, yeah. He's not from New Orleans.
Did you know Frankie Gibbs out there, a trombone player, a cripple?
Frankie Gibbs, no.
He used to work with Lazy Daddy.
Houston Bucket, I know him too. He used to work with him.
Punch was talking about him. Punch did, yeah.
No, I don't, I don't remember him now.
What about Chris Kelly and Jack Carey, those fellas?
Well, I worked with them for a while. I worked with Jack Carey for a while. Just like I was telling you, I worked with them on gigs, you know? Chris Kelly, I worked with them on gigs.
And who was in Jack Carey's band? Different fellas or was it pretty scary or what?

I know Black Happy was the drummer. Jack Carey played trombone. Who else played? I don't know who was playing trumpet. Lee, yeah, Lee Collin played with him for a while. I can't think of the bass player. I used to work also with Duke and Forstay. You ever heard of Trombone Play by the name of Forstay?

And Duke and his two brothers? The brother played trumpet? Yeah. He used to work with Joe Avery and Wilbur Tilma when I first came in 1945. He died. I have a private recording of the mother's play, you know, in Mayden. For me, just for something to remember him by when I was a young lady. He played nice.
Well, yeah, he used to be the nice of the nightclub.
Who was the first time to remember?

I'll tell you who used to play bass with Jack Carey for a while. Al Morgan. Yeah, Al Morgan used to play it too. And that's funny thing, Al Morgan both played, he had Isaiah Morgan and there was another Morgan, there was a trumpet player, and they used to have a band, you know, each one had a band, but Al Morgan never did play with either one of his brothers. He was working with Jack Carey, I think he worked with Chris Kelly, just gigging around with different guys.

Isaiah had a struggle with... Oh yeah? He's up in Biloxi. He comes in to see Sam's wife at all. Oh yeah. They all keep in touch. Who was in Chris Kelly? That's kind of hard for me to remember. I forgot a lot of those guys. You mentioned the drum roll player.

Yeah, what's his name? Jim Robinson. Jim Robinson was one of those guys in Chris Kelly's band. This is another one. Everybody calls him by his nickname. Who did you go to Pensacola with when you first left?
We went to Pensacola with Buddy, Petit, Chani, we had Ray Chani on drums, we had Al Morgan on bass,

Earl Lumpfords, trombone, clarinet. Little fella, I can't think of his last name. His name was Manny. That's all I can think of. What did you mention? Banjo player. He was a kid too, by the way. We had to get permission from his father to take him along with us. And what happened over there? Well, we stayed there for quite a while and I think it got a little tough. Buddy Petit came back to New Orleans, Earl Lumpfords came back. So we got another trumpet player by the name of her, Mac Thomas, to play trumpet. And we also got a piano player, a woman piano player, played with us. We picked up in Pensacola, Florida. What was her name? Helen, I can't think of her last name, but I think finally that the trumpet player, Mac Thomas, finally did marry her.
Was she related to Sadie? You know Sadie that used to play around here? She might have come after you left. Sadie Goodson, Clarice Goodson. She's a New York man, but you might have known.
No.
She had a whole lot of good women in piano players. What about George Morris? Who was he?

George Morris was a trombone playing the band. He was there. After Buddy Petit left, well, George Morris took the band over. He happened to be there. I think he's from New Orleans, too, this George Morris. So he happened to be there. We made him the leader of the band, this George Morris. I see.
And after you played around there for a while, did you stay in Florida? Did you come back?

I'll tell you the story. After being in Pensacola, Florida, then we decided to make a tour of Florida. We went down to Jacksonville, Florida. So when we was in Jacksonville, Florida, I met a fellow there by the name of Eagle Eye Shields. So he liked what I was doing, so he asked me, he said, anytime you want to, anytime things get tough with you, you want to come down to Jacksonville. He had all to go down to Jacksonville anyway. He said, come on down, let me know, and we can get together. I'll put you in my band, okay? So, you know, we went back to Pensacola, Florida. I'll never forget, we was in Mobile, Alabama. We had a couple of days off. Things got a little tough. So I thought about this Eagle Eye Shields. So I wrote him a letter. And I told somebody in the band, I said, well, if this guy is me in business, I'm going to ask him for some money. So I asked him for $50. The next day I got the $50. So I said, well, this guy is me in business. So I went on down. He paid my way, train, fare and everything. So I went on down to Jacksonville, Florida. And I stayed with his band for, oh, quite a long time. Because he used to do all his own booking. There was no booking agent then, you know? So there was another fellow in Jacksonville, Florida, had a band by the name of Alonzo Ross. So he was working in Miami, Florida. But he was originally from Jacksonville and he heard me playing so he wanted me to play with his band now in Miami, Florida. So I told him, I said, so I'm a little ahead of my story. But anyway, by being in Jacksonville, Florida, so we wanted a trumpet player. If you remember, it was a, we were talking about a trumpet player just a while ago by the name of Anderson. He had all the go. He was working with Eagle Eye Shield then. At that time, this fellow by the name of Broadway Jones from New York used to go down to Miami, Florida. As a singer. So he decided he'd take a band to New York. So he took the trumpet player from Eagle Eye Shield's band. So he was stuck with trumpet player. So he asked me where could we get a trumpet player and I recommend Cootie, Cootie Williams. That's how Cootie Williams left Mobile, Alabama. So I got permission from his father, being a kid. So we had him to come down to Jacksonville. So he joined the band, see. So after Alonzo Ross wanted me to join his band, so I told him, I got a kid I got to look out for, which is Cootie Williams. So if you can make room for him, we'll join your band. So next couple of days, I got a letter from Ross, say, I'll make room for Cootie. So I said, well, this is it. So Cootie and I joined Alonzo Ross' band. So Alonzo Ross was making a tour of Florida, and so when he came through Jacksonville, we joined his band, so then, well, the only, I think he was working nine months out of a year down in Miami, Florida. So when he went down to Florida, next time to Miami, we went through. From there, Victor is scouting around for musician. You know what I mean, band. We had some original tune. So we were touring Georgia. And if you remember, it was a band by the name of Black Steel. Blue Steel. Blue Steel. Was it Blue Steel or Black Steel? Something like that. And if you remember years of one of the things, you remember that, that tune, Girl of My Dreams? Yeah. Well, it was written by one of the guys in that band. The Blue Steel? Yeah. And Victor wanted that particular tune. Well, he wouldn't sell it to him unless his band would record it. So they sent a portable set down to Savannah, Georgia, and they recorded the tune. And we was in Savannah, Georgia, and we had some original tune, so the next day we, Alonzo, a band, recorded for Victor. For, in the, so when the record came out, the guy at the Roseland Bar, I mean, he heard the record. He's looking for talent. So he sent for the band to come to New York. And that's how we got to New York. And I've been there ever since, 1928.
I was wondering if you knew any people around there, like, just blues piano players around Savannah and Jacksonville, like Sugar Underwood? Sugar Underwood, yeah, I remember him.
I remember Sugar Underwood, yeah. Was he working with bands any, or was it just solo?
No, no, just solo.
He was one of them guys playing all the tough keys, you know. You mean all the black keys? All the black keys.
I know, I know. Well that's easy, you don't have to get your fingers. Yeah, you put your fingers between playing all the black keys and it was tough to follow
that guy. And he was a good piano player too. Very good. Yeah, I heard the record, somebody played a record of him.
Do you know what's happened to him? No.
It'd be nice to find out. I don't know.

I don't know. I don't know. Did you know Blind Mac, by any chance, he played piano and sang around Jacksonville? I doubt if you would, he just played blues, played pretty nice. I don't know. I guess all the things on Lonnie Johnson's own style singing. Some of the people are, you know, I don't know. Some of the people that you worked with in New York, got a player, different bands.

Well, different bands, I worked with quite a few different bands. I worked with, let's see, can I get them in rotation? When you first got there, I was thinking about you. When I first got there, well, I went there with Ross's band. We only stayed on the job about two weeks. Then I went into a dancing school with another, by the way it was a piano player down in Florida that was in New York. He went to New York with this Broadway gentleman. So when we got to New York and working at a big place like the Roseland, it's used to call it a Rosemont, that was in Brooklyn. And it happened, so we was playing opposite the Indiana Five. And we got ten men and there's only five guys and those guys were really playing. They made us sound bad for a while, you know. So we didn't like, Ross seems to be one of the weakest guys in the band, so we got this piano player Arthur Ford to play for us and Mick Ross the leader. But we only stayed on the job about two weeks and I went to dancing school. Coot and I got an offer right away to play in the dancing school and with this piano player Arthur Ford. So we went to the dancing school, had a little four piece band and I stayed there for about over a year. Then I left there and went with another band by the name of Charlie Skeet working in the dance with saxophone and clarinet and all that.
Then Charlie Skeet, we got rid of him and got Claude Hopkins in the band.

That's how that started, Claude Hopkins band. That's how that started and went to the Savoy Ballroom, pretty good band. So when they hired us in the Savoy Ballroom, Chick Webb Band was at the Savoy, so they went down to the Roseland Mall. So happened to the manager, happened to come in to Savoy and he said you'd rather have Claude Hopkins band than Chick Webb Band. That's how we got into the Roseland Mall. We Claude Hopkins band. Do you know Geechee Fields? Traumhole player? Traumhole player. Yeah, I don't know too much about him, I remember him. Geechee Fields, yeah. I just wondered if you knew what had happened to him.
No. I heard he's still around New York, I think it was three or four years.
Oh yeah?
Sure, I remember he was. Sure. He was supposed to have been with that Charlie Skeet's band.
Well yeah, he was with Charlie Skeet's band for a while, but that was before I got rid of the band.
Who was a trombone player when you were there?

We didn't have no trombone player with Charlie Skeet. After I got, we had three saxophones, two trumpet, bass, piano and drum, and guitar, four rhythm. Well who was the bass player? What's his name? You know his name? Henry Turner. Was that Nick Turner?
No.
No, his name is Henry Turner.
There's a bass player that used to play around Texas with Don Alba called Henry Nick Turner, and he doubles on trombone.
No, that's just another, just another fellow. He worked with Don Alba.
He made those recordings with Don Alba, but I don't know if you've ever heard of him or not.
No, this guy was a bass player and also used to play, he played a tuba too. Yeah.
It might be the same fella, Mike Donald. I just thought I'd check. Bill, maybe we could get him to just tell everybody hello.

Yeah, the trouble is the tape is down near the end there now, and that's when the machine starts slowing down. Alright, well we'll wait, we'll wait till we get a new tape. We'll get on a new reel in just a minute. You've got a couple more questions there, though. Oh, I was going to ask something about your clarinet style, which is that original, you know, that good tone you got there that's really got some real guts to it. What? How do you do that? Or what, where did you first get onto that? I mean, you know, I mean it's really, you know, a punch to it.

I didn't practice anything about it, I don't know, it's just, that's the way, huh? It's just, yeah, it just come to me, I don't, you know what I mean, no, I just picked it up how I did it, I don't know.
Did you do that way back when you were back here, started out? Yeah, I don't know, I got to. I got to.

tendency to get that kind of a, I don't know what you'd call it, a harsh tone or a certain tune you play, you know, it just comes to you. But one thing bad about it, if you do too much you can't stop it, you see. So I just, I don't know, I just play whatever comes to my mind, the way I feel.

You do it with your, by using a different type of reed? No, no, that come from your throat. You do it with your throat? Yeah. You start to use your vocal cords, yeah? That's right, yeah. That's right. Hum with it a little bit. Yeah. I knew some players could do it that way, I didn't know if you did it that way.
Yeah, it come from your throat, you make it sound rash, like you know. Like playing blues, that fits in a little. Yeah, but if you play in a nice ballad, that wouldn't go. Yeah, sure.
Well, how hard a reed do you use?
Well, I'm using a lavas, I'm using a medium hard.
And in the old age, did you use very hard or something?
No, well, in the old days, you know, it's not like, all your reads now, practically the number now, you see. The old days, you just had to pick out until you get a good one.
And did you try for a hard one or a soft one?
No, well, I guess medium.
Yeah. Did you do anything until you read? No. What you got?
You just... No, just...
What about your mouthpiece?
Well, to be frankly, I only used three mouthpieces in my whole life, since I've been playing.
Did you open up that?
No.
No.
Just leave it. Just leave it just a while. You buy them open now or close, see. So, do you still use Albert? Albert's system kind. You always did use Albert?
Always did.

Well, I got a, I have a new one, but it's still Albert's system. What make you use? I'm using, well this is the first time I've been using a Selma now for about a year. When we was on this tour in Europe, I bought a Selma, I went to the factory and I bought
a Selma.
Paris, yeah.
They still make Albert's system?
No, it just happened so that this guy happened to have one in the factory. So, he said, I only have one. So, he went and got it. I was lucky and I got this lesson.
Do you remember what you started on? What kind of clarinet it was? Albert's system?
What do you mean? Not the name. What the make? No, I don't know what the make was.
There were a lot of them in those days. Oh, yeah. Did you ever use a buffet? Buffet?

Yeah. I was using a buffet because the one that I, this Selma client that I bought in France, it cracked on him, see? I had to have it fixed. So, it happened to, I was also using a penzamala when I was waiting at the cafe. So, Jimmy Dawson came in the place one night. So, the penzamala company gave him the clarinet, see? So, he came in and he wanted to sit down and play. I said, well, I don't know. I said, I'm using a penzamala and I said, this thing is in bad shape. So, he said, well, I have a buffet you can use and take it out to the factory and have it fixed. I used that buffet. By the way, I have that buffet now. I gave it back to him. And so, when this clarinet cracked that I have now, I went to him, he, I'm using, I still have his buffet. But, I had mine fixed and I haven't returned his buffet yet. So, I got him just before I left to come here. From where? From some fella, he's a old man, he's 80 years old, he's a retired symphony man. He had two beautiful bouffés, A and a B. I just got him, he said, I just hope somebody can get some use out of them and they're really beautiful.
Did you ever use an A clarinet or just everything on B flat usually?
No, I used one A clarinet and that was, I made a recording with, with Mud Carey. You know, about 67 years ago. Yeah, those rags.
Yeah, all those rags.
Choplin rags. Choplin rags. And I had to use an A clarinet and I had a time finding one. I finally got one. And we made a recording with an A clarinet.
What about C clarinet in E class?
No, I never did.
You ever play parades much in the old days? Oh yeah, yeah, sure.
And you used a B clarinet on A clarinet? No, no, I used to use a C. I had a C. C and parades. Yeah, that's right. Who did you work with on the street? Some of the different bands?
Buddy, Gus. Buddy P.T.? Buddy P.T., Gus Madcat, Chris Kelly, whoever would get a parade or get an advertisement, get that gig, we'd play. Sure.
Do you have anything you want to tell the people in particular? Any advice to young clarinetists maybe?
Well, all I can tell them is just practice and keep playing, that's all I can say. Because that's what I had to do, I had to do a lot of practicing. Buddy.
Do you think any trumpet players influence your clarinet style?

Yeah. Buddy P.T. Buddy. He's the first trumpet player I ever heard spoke about different chords. Minor, major, augmented, you know. He was actually a musician. At that particular time bands used to follow his policy. Just like, you know, one band has got all the gold, the rest of the band used to follow, right man? I said, well Buddy is playing a, I remember the time like we played new tunes, he'd go down there to some music store right on the canal, and he'd go get a piano copy. You know, I didn't play it off, the rest of the guys would catch it. And that's how we used to get the new tunes, and other bands would pick up the tunes as we'd play them. Sure.
Did Buddy run the chords straight up and down?
Yeah, oh yeah, he knows his instrument. He knew his chords. Oh yeah, he knew his chords. He knew his chords, he could read. Sure.
Did he have any special way of playing the chords so he could get those very instruments?
No, I don't think so. He's the one that started me off. He's the one that was, he was my inspiration, to start to play music.
Did he use any special thing right in the trumpet player?
I don't think so, no. He ever used newts much?
Oh yeah, well that Brown Derby he used to use, instead of using, you know, like he used to use your hand, he'd take his Derby and fan his horn, you know. Yeah, he was very famous for that.
Did he ever cock his valves a little long?
His half valves halfway down, you know, with sliding glissandles like Louis does.
No, I think Punch Miller used to be a shock on that half cock valve.
Did you work much with Punch down here?

By the way, on that Jack Carey, that's who was the trumpet player mostly, Lee Collins and Punch Miller. Punch Miller was one of the Jack Carey famous trumpet players. I couldn't think of the trumpet players. See?
Did you work any panels of music?
Battle of music?
For a cock or anything like that? No. Never did. Riverboat? The riverboat?

No, I never, I was, I was fortunate I never did get on one of those riverboats. The first time I ever played with one of these riverboats here from New Orleans was, I was working with Claude Hopkins and we happened to be going through St. Louis. The boat happened to be in St. Louis and we played a dance on the boat.
That's good, I don't think there was any noise. Did you know Mud down here by the way, Mud Carey? No. You met Mud Carey?
I met, I met Mud, the first time I met Mud was in New York. And that was the time that we made this recording. I heard about him because he was in California because he came to New York for a while.
He's gone out there with our Aggies, man, in 1919. Yeah.
You may have those records through that, maybe. I like that. We got them all.
You have them all, huh?
No way. There's one of them I have.
Well not all of them, we got half of them.
Half of them, there's one of them I haven't got. We made a tune by the name of African Misk. Have you got that one? No.
I have them on there. I don't know if it's ever been issued out of them.
If I can find it, I'll try to find it and send it to them. Okay, I don't remember the title.
Because that's the one I think I used that e-clarinet on you spoke about just one.

Oh, it was one of them with Mud Carey. Oh, there is a new one they brought out. It could be on that one. It could be on that new one. Which I was going to go and get this afternoon, we didn't get time. But there's a new one on Savoy now, that same Mud Carey section, and they call it Volume 2. I don't know what's on it, but I'll find out. Volume 2, maybe it's in it. It might be this time. Something they didn't issue the first time.
Was it a Red Book number? That's right, a Red Book.

I have those Red Books I was just showing, Dick. Oh, yeah. They belonged to Bunk, you know. That's right. They had photosites made for Bunk, and then they came over and borrowed them. So Pop Foster had them, too. Yeah, that's right. Pop Foster came over and got them from Bunk.
Did they use the Red Book much down here when you were here?
No, because practically all these tunes that everybody knew them, you know, so many bands play them, you know. They said we didn't use them. Did Buddy read pretty well? Yeah, Buddy was a musician.
Yeah. You think he's one of the greatest, or maybe the greatest one that would make you pick on the spot.
Yeah, but in my estimation, he is, he is the, he was the guy for trumpet.
Did he play any other instrument to get his ear developed?
Not that I know of. Not that I know of.
I was wondering, because he seemed to know the chords and everything, I thought that he studied it.

No, I don't know what his father, I don't know what his father, was his people any musician or not, but I don't know where he got it from, but he was a good musician. I don't know where he got it from, where he picked it up.
Well, we don't want to keep you, I know you have other things to do. Oh, I have time. I just don't think of it. Hey Dad, this is a pleasure.
I'm relaxing now.
Anything else about Buddy Petit that we can think of? Did he play high or low? No, no, no, no.
He wasn't, he didn't play too high. He was always right there in the staff, you know, and he really, he's a really good player.

If we never heard him, we would have somebody, we would have to ask all these foolish questions, but since we didn't, we wonder sometimes how he did sound. Did he play somewhat like Louis' style, you think? Well, except Louis, of course, plays high now. Yeah. But I mean, do you think, it was a nice mellow tone?

Yeah, he had a nice tone. Well, to be frank with the way he played, he seemed, you could tell that he was, he was well schooled. You know what he was doing. He knew his instrument. There's no question about that. That's the thing that, yeah, kind of got me arrested, you know?
What about Oliver? He used a lot of mutes.

Well, Oliver, well I didn't know too much, I didn't know too much about Joe Oliver. I didn't know too much, I heard him several times because he came out the reserve when I was a kid and played Kid Ory, Oliver, Baby Dots, Johnny Dots, and that bunch, you know, I heard him. But, by the pity, I worked with him and I know what he could do.

And you played real pretty though, wasn't it? Oh yeah. He didn't try to get a lot of the freak effects and things like that out of the horn, mostly a real pretty mellow tone. Did he play loud ever? No, he didn't play too loud.
Oh, above the staff, never.
Yeah, he's on the order, well I'm telling you, Bobby Hackett was on that order. You know, nothing loud, just, just no instruments. Played a lot of feeling.
Well, how would he compare with Chris Kelly?
Oh, he was way trumpet playing Chris Kelly. Maybe Chris Kelly could hit a lot of higher notes than he can. But he actually, oh, he wasn't, Chris Kelly wasn't even in his class. I don't think so.
Did Chris have more variations or less?

Well, he was much, I mean, he was much more powerful than this Buddy PT. You know, he could blow louder and everything. But for knowing his instrument, I think Buddy was, yeah. What about Kid Rene? Did you hear him when you... Yeah, Kid Rene was another guy in his time, could do a lot of playing too, but he wasn't, he was louder than Buddy. Because all of them came up just about that same time, Kid Rene, Buddy PT, Lois Armstrong, Joe Oliver was just before that time. Because Joe Oliver, I don't know when he left and went to, I think he was, when I came to New Orleans, I think Joe Oliver was in Chicago.

Did you ever know Blond Freddy, a clarinet player by that name? Blond Freddy, no. Did you ever know Isidore Fritz, who's from out in the country somewhere? Isidore Fritz, huh? I just wondered how those fellas played, and we don't have any records of them. Blond Freddy's still alive, but he doesn't play clarinet. No, no, I don't know them. Who does Jack Carey play like on one of the other ones?

Play like Jack Carey, I guess. They used to call him, by you know they changed his name, they used to call him Tiger Rag. And all they changed, they tuned Tiger Rag to Jack Carey. When they wanted Tiger Rag, they said, play Jack Carey, and he used to do some kind of triple tug in that Tiger Rag, and everybody used to go for that.
There's nobody around today that you think compares with him?
With who? With Jack Carey's style.
With, you know, with Jack Carey. Did O'Replay it all like him?
Well, yeah, on that same order, but Jack Carey was noted for that Tiger Rag. Tiger Rag, that was his famous tune. He made his name through that, playing that Tiger Rag.

What about Morris French? Did you know him, a trombone player? Morris French? No. He's up around La Posse now, I thought they knew him. What's his name? Morris French. No. He used to work with Louis and Papa Salas. Morris French? No, I don't know him. That's the word before you put about some of your brothers, because most people, you're the famous one, and probably some of your brothers were pretty good too.
Yeah, well I have Mount Woolley's brother, Robert, he was, he was one of them, he was a really good musician. He used to play tenor, played clarinet, I think he played a little piano.
He can do something with a bass, a little trombone, he can do a little everything.
Is he a good get-off man?
Yeah, that's what's good. During those days he used to be playing.
Does he play at all?
No, I don't think he's playing anymore.
Are you playing anymore?
He play every now and then, play ten. Every now and then he get a gig, just play just mostly for kicks. Because he's working for the government now.
What about Edward?

Edward is the only one who didn't play anything. Edward didn't play no instrument. But Clarence, Clarence played baritone, I think he played a little Clarence, Herbert, he played Clarence and saxophone. Did you do a sister sing? My sister used to sing. My father was a musician. I had a couple of uncles, a guitar player, and I had one also uncle, a trumpet player. What was his name? Do you remember? His name, uh, Gilles, huh? His nickname was Gilles. We used to call him, his last name was Dewey, huh? We used to call him Piran, I don't know, he's French accent. Dewey?
Could he be related to Lawrence Dewey? Yeah, we all related.
Lawrence Dewey, Dr. Dewey. Sure.
I know Lawrence, I haven't seen him for three or four years. He's still out in La Fiesta. Yeah.
Clarence is playing music.
Yeah, Clarence is still playing.
Clarence played gig in my own.
I think he's waking tomorrow night at the time. I like to hear him come back on Suprano. He played that one day. Who was that, Clarence? Clarence. There's not many Suprano players left.
Well Sidney Bashier, Sidney Bashier, he's still playing that piano.
I play that Suprano. He left before you left. Oh yeah, he left before what?

After your buddy and a lot of those guys spoke about Sidney Bashier. Because they say he take a piano playing a drum and this is a soprano and go out on a clown and go out on a truck and give this band. He always, I always just like his playing. He always.
You were in New York?
Huh?
You were in New York?

Yeah. I met him after he came back from Europe. I think it was after the war he came back with Noble Sisters of the Band. Yeah. That's when I first met him. Yeah. I met him. I was a guest of his in France when I was there last time.
Who did your brothers play with?

Some of them in the band. Do you remember? Robert used to play with this same trauma. I was talking about, you see, you're going to look up Gus Madcat for a long time. And Herbert played with some band out in Texas. I don't know what his name was. Don Albert? Don Albert. Don Albert. He worked with a couple of bands.
With Alvin Alcorn? Yeah. That's right. I've got a record that plays baritone. Louis Padreau was playing clarinet.

Yeah. He played baritone, he played tenor, played clarinet. He's playing most of the clarinet. He's playing baritone too? Yeah. He's mostly playing clarinet now. He went to Europe with a bunch of guys from New York.
Did anybody work? Yeah.
Was it another one of that?
Yeah. Was it another one of that? What was that?
Europe?
Yeah. Oh, we were talking about the old days.
You're talking about the old days? That's not, this is just recent. You don't want the present.

Well, it's so hard to get a history on some of these people, you know. And he's got to remember how they play. There's so few people who even know that Buddy Petite is. He's got such a reason. And he's like that.
That's why we were trying to put you on the spot, but we were trying to wonder sort of what style, you know, he plays and all.
Well, Buddy Petite was like a leader in the trumpet field. The guys used to follow him. He was also a drummer too I used to work with by the name of Red Dugas. You ever heard of him?
Never. Was he from here?
Yeah, right from here, no. Red Dugas. He was during Basin Street, right down Human Canal Street.
Whose band was he with? His own?

Yeah, he used to have a band of his own, Picker Band. You know, during those times we wouldn't take a study job. It was only a few study jobs. The first study job I ever worked on with Buddy Petite, that was the one in Covington, Louisiana. That was for a few weeks. Then from there we went on, we went to Galveston, Texas. And we served there for about three months. And we went on to the first time we ever had a study job. A lot of musicians at that time wouldn't take a study job. You could make no money to take a job. But you'd gig in every night, you know, like we'd play here. Tomorrow night we'd play in Biloxi, Mandeville, Covington, you know, go around.
Did you know Bunk Johnson?
No, I didn't know Bunk Johnson at that time.
How about the problem with his story of Robin?
I didn't know too much about him, Pico. Oh, Pico. Yeah. He used to, my brother lived right next to me. Yeah. Still plays. Oh yeah. Seems really good to have.
Are there any other clarinet players you remember as being outstanding when you first got to town? Or in the country? No.

It was a, it was a fellow from Baton Rouge used to play with some band from Baton Rouge. He's the one of those guys that I see didn't use the sharp and flat key. He just had to, just used the six hole, C natural and B natural. All the rest of the keys he took them off and stopped them up and played any key. Yeah. And how he did it I don't know. I don't remember his name. I heard him one night and he could play it.
Whose band would he work with? I don't know, some band. Could it have been Toots Johnson or Victor or something like that?
Toots Johnson was a trumpet player?
Yeah.
From Baton Rouge.
Heavyset. Yeah, I've heard of him. That's right. And who he was, Toots Johnson's band. Who was that one's on? Miami. From here.
Oh, you're talking about Punch Miller. No, he's something.
Oh yeah, well we got him with Jack Carey.
Punch was up there two nights ago. Yeah. He's been around town since last fall.
Who was that one's on the bell? Oh, it is.

I met him after I got in Florida. And we were just trying to check on some of the older New Orleans history that other people wouldn't know. Because it's been a long time since we've seen you and you've been back here. We remember a lot of those fellas. Right around now. Well, we don't want to keep you on that one.
One more question about your father. When do you think he started playing jazz or did he ever play real jazz?

Not to be frank with you. I never heard him play with any band, but he used to pick up his own and just run exercise. But from what I can understand, they had a pretty nice band. I spoke to one of the fellas. He died last year. He's the only one out of 18 of them. He was the only one living. He was the tuba player. And he lived out in the country and I had a chance to speak to him. So, because he was losing his eyesight. And when he found out that, you know, who I was, he couldn't see. And I asked him a story about, I want to find out about my father when they went to New York and everything. That was, that was, what, 1953. And he remembered, now that was 63 years ago that they'd been in New York, he remembered the address, the right address, the street, how many days they stayed in New York. He also, the Pickwood band? No, no. Was it the Pickwood or the Ornwood? Whatever. It was one of them. But anyway, the one that left, it was a big festival going on in New York and every state sent a band. So this band from here is the one that won the first prize. And he was telling the whole story about what happened. He also had his horn, he said he had the music, some tune that they won the first prize on, I think a tune called Echo. And he told me that his daughter had it. And pictures of the band, so I had to leave to go back to New York in the hurry, so I could get my sister, get in touch with his daughter. And she said she'd been moved so much she can't find the music or the pictures, but she had the horn. It's a horn that he used to play.

It would be interesting to know if they were playing ear music, any of them, how early, if you could determine how early his father was playing about ear. They was playing my ear? I don't know. Because you know they always set different dates for the origin of jazz. Jazz, yeah. But the more people I talk to, the earlier it gets.

I tell you the experience I had, a lot of people come up to me and ask me why I play an Album System clarinet. So I say well when I started they wasn't making a BAM System clarinet. Well I was wrong, I was just guessing because I had never seen a BAM clarinet before, you see. So, the year before last when I went to France, I went to the Selma factory and I just happened to be talking to the, to the owner of the factory. Absolutely.
I might as well. I would thank you.

And so I say I want a question, I want you to tell me something. Yes, no. I said, people have been asking me why I play Album System clarinet. I'm just guessing I tell them that, well when I started playing they wasn't making a BAM System clarinet. He said, how long you been playing? I told him, he said, well you mistaken. So he said, BAM clarinet was made way back in 1853. So he said, wait a while. So he goes in the factory and comes back with the clarinet, the first BAM clarinet was made. And I said, this is the first BAM clarinet was made. My father made it, my father made it in 1853. This is the first one ever was made that he shot it. So I said, well, higher on than I get. So from now on when they ask that question, I know the answer to that now.
You just happen to have more Alberts around.
Yeah, that's right.
Have you ever tried BAM?
I tried several times on the color. My fingers are so large and you know, it's so much closer. So I didn't include, I could just as much out of my Alberts as I would get on the BAM.
Think there's any difference in the tone some people think and the others?
Yes, it is. I think so.
You like the Alberts?

I rather the tone of an Alberts for different bands. Now playing with a combination of six-piece common Dixieland bands, I don't think a BAM clarinet fits in there. Because the tone is beautiful, rich and everything, but it haven't got the big tone when you get, especially when you get in the lower register.
Everybody I always liked, like Noon and Dodds and the old timers, they most of them have a big tone on that.
A big tone, you get a bigger tone out of, I think, out of an Alberts system kind of than you do a BAM.

And to me, for tonguing and execution, for really fast execution, Jimmy Noon made it. I mean anything you want to make it. There's no point in playing any faster than him, huh? And there's anybody who can do it faster than him to play the perfect tonguing. Yeah, well he was very famous on tonguing. And he had execution, sure, on way, way back, when you were just starting. I know I can hear those old records, and he was making it on Alberts.

I have a friend of mine in Hartford, Connecticut, he's a symphony man, he's in his sixties. So he wanted to know, how in the world can I get over that Alberts system so fast? I play a solo on clarinet marmalade, and I play it fast, just as fast as he can hear it. The faster they play, the better I like it. And he wanted to know, how in the world can I get over an Alberts system so fast? And I said, well I can play clarinet marmalade, I've been playing it so much, I can play clarinet marmalade and think of something that happened twenty years ago. They can't play it too fast.
Did the bands play fast in the old days?
No, no, we never played nothing fast.
Could you beat off some about the right tempo for them as fast as they played?

Well now? In the old days? In the old days everything was, every, the hard, let's see, was it. Like Tiger Rags, for instance? Tiger Rags was about the fastest thing they would play. How would they stop it off? It wasn't too fast. But now today I just pick up that, I never could play nothing fast until I got with Terry Wilson started picking up that fast because he played piano and you know he'd feature in the band, he liked everything up, you know. So I got so used to that and all.

I was going to ask again about the Alberts system. They don't have as many keys usually as the BAME. Do you think that makes it easier to slide from one note to the other by not having too many rings and keys? Or do you like to have as many keys and rings as possible on it? No, I'm making slurs, Bill. Yeah, like when you, you know, I mean does it seem more like a vocal quality to you? Can you do more with it as far as the fingering, the extra keys that the game has, do they hold you back with your finger? What, the BAME system? Yeah, they sometimes have more keys.

I don't know, well maybe, but because I never did play a BAME system so I, you know. Yeah, I would never work on that. But that Albert system, I think I can get anything. I'll tell you one thing I find out, I find out that certain passage is better to make on the Albert system than the BAME and it's just the opposite run too. Because you take an Albert system, your artificial fingering on it starts after you hit C sharp. But on a BAME your artificial fingering starts after you make B natural. Up high. Up high, yeah. Up high. But that make it, you got more artificial fingering on that, on that, on that BAME than you have on that, on that Albert.
What about, did they use two beat in the old days, a straight four or what, when you first came to New Orleans?
No, they was using two beats. They was using two beats. They was using two beats.
Who do you think introduced four? Or did they ever introduce you there when you were here?

No, they wasn't. Four beat wasn't introduced. Only some drummers would use four beats sometimes, like on the last chorus going out, he would go to four. But everybody was using two beats. Sometimes when you get to that last chorus everybody's shouting, then you'd go to four beats. What about real slow blues?
Did anybody ever play four on that?

No, I don't remember anybody playing four on the slow blues. I'll tell you another thing, when I went to New York everybody was playing tuba in a regular dance band. You know what we were with stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff

they'd use a string bass. I was surprised to see them, but one band I think that I knew that was using a string band, that was Duke Hamilton. Bro happened to be playing that, and he was playing bass violin, but all the rest of the band was playing tubas.
Did they use banjos much here?
Banjo? Yeah, it was one kind of thing that, it was banjo, then it changed to guitar, and then everybody went back to banjo.
What was the piano?

Piano and all that came, we never did know nothing about no piano. We started, we did know piano, because we could sit up anywhere in the street, because the guitar, play all the banjo, they had this instrument with them.
It'd be hard to play some of those picnics with a piano.

With a piano, sure, you didn't have to have no piano. It was one piano player here that I know that used to play with a dance man, I don't know his last name, he used to be called Steve, who was working with... Steve Lewis. Steve, what's his name, Steve Lewis. Steve Lewis.
Yeah.
He used to always play like this. Yeah, that's right.
With a two fingers, yeah.
That's Steve Lewis. And he was working, playing piano with... With this guy? Pierron.
Pierron. Yeah. He recorded with him, he signed by. Yeah.
And on the wagons too, they couldn't get a piano on that thing.
They do sometimes. Yeah.
A big truck that they have.

He recorded with New Orleans' Willie Jackson. He made a great song called Old New Orleans Blues, if you ever get a chance to hear that. Steve Lewis with New Orleans' Willie Jackson. Steve Lewis, yeah.
Well, I didn't know him, I just saw him off the distance.

Yeah. It's really nice. Something you should hear. I mean, it's got nice sentiment in it, you know. It describes a town. Good town. We were just about out of tape here. Yeah, I thought we were. I thought you might remember New Orleans' Willie Jackson, he used to entertain at that.
Willie Jackson, I heard the name, I don't know.
Tom Anderson, he was an entertainer there with another phone.
Tom Anderson, that's right up, that's right up here on Rampart Street, isn't it?
Yeah. Nookie Johnson, I knew all that Willie Jackson, I think. Two guys.
What's the name of the place you said? Tom Anderson. Tom Anderson, isn't it on Rampart Street? Rampart and Arbavilla, I think.
Yeah.

Just a few doors from Canal Street? Yeah, that's right. Right in the middle of the block. Armstrong used to work there too? Yeah. Barney Big Garden. That's the first place I heard Armstrong. It was at Tom Anderson. At that time he was using a piano, drums, I think Zutty was drumming with him, and the trumpet. And every night when we'd come. Piano player? Huh? I don't know who was the piano player, Tom. Because that night when we'd come from gigging we had to, I don't know, we had to change, right here on Rampart and Canal Street. We'd get off the streetcar if we were coming from downtown and we'd come over and listen at him, play for a while, wait for the car to come to go uptown.
Do you know Udell Wilson, did you ever know him? No. I think he's from Kansas City and he played around.
Udell, no, I heard the name, I don't know him.
He worked with Louis on piano, so I'm Ian Zutty, working a trio, I just wondered, it might be the same. You can ask Louis. Yeah. What's the name, I heard that name?
Udell Wilson. Udell Wilson. Yeah, because I don't think Lil Umtong didn't join him before he got to Chicago. She's from Memphis. She's from Memphis, yeah.

I was going to ask one more question. Do you think the music of the churches, the songs, the spirituals, ever influenced the jazz bands much? I think so. Do you think kids go to church and hear that music? Yeah, I think so.

I think the thing that they call rock and roll right now, I've been hearing that for years, I used that in the Sanctified Church, these people have been doing that for years, but now the bands are playing in it. That's what it is, rock and roll, that's all rock and roll is.
Did you grow up in a particular church? Which church were you a member?
No, no, all my people were Catholic. Never Catholic? Yeah.
You never heard that type of number?
No, I didn't. It was spiritual. I used to hear the other churches when it's saying. You hear some of that?
Yeah, I hear some of that.
Sure.

segments.summary: Hall's guitar-playing uncle, and how he and his brother began on guitar before switching to the clarinet their father handed out.

segments.title: First job with the Thomas band in Reserve
segments.summary: Hall recalls his first band, a group of kids around Reserve, and struggles to name the drummer, bassist and trombonist.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: First New Orleans jobs with Bud Roussel and Lee Collins
segments.summary: After coming to New Orleans Hall joins Bud Roussel's band with trumpeter Lee Collins, and also plays with Gus Metcalf and drummer Black Happy.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Joining Buddy Petit's band and its members
segments.summary: Hall recalls how he joined Buddy Petit, the 1920 Covington photo, Gus Metcalf's pick-up bands, and Petit's sidemen.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Early idols: Jimmy Noone, Tio, Piron and Robichaux
segments.summary: Asked who influenced him on arrival, Hall names Jimmy Noone and Lorenzo Tio, and recalls Robichaux's New York trip and Piron.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Buddy Petit's tunes and the origin of Tin Roof Blues
segments.summary: Hall lists Petit's repertoire and says Petit composed Tin Roof Blues, with the tune's original name discussed.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Touring after Covington and Petit's appearance
segments.summary: The band tours Alabama and Mississippi with an agent, and Hall and Allen describe Petit's puffed cheeks, brown derby and looks.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Houston, Galveston and Lake Charles with pianist Lazy Daddy
segments.summary: The Petit band goes to Houston and Galveston, hires pianist Lazy Daddy, and splits up in Lake Charles; talk of Lazy Daddy's background.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Gigging with Jack Carey and Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Hall describes gigs with Jack Carey and Chris Kelly, their sidemen, and the Morgan brothers.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
segments.title: Pensacola with Buddy Petit and George Morris
segments.summary: Hall lists the band that went to Pensacola, who stayed or left, and George Morris taking over as leader.

segments.title: Eagle Eye Shields in Jacksonville and Alonzo Ross
segments.summary: Hall writes Eagle Eye Shields for money, joins his band in Jacksonville, and is recruited by Alonzo Ross for Miami.

segments.title: Sugar Underwood and Florida blues pianists
segments.summary: Allen asks about blues pianists around Savannah and Jacksonville, notably Sugar Underwood, who played in all the black keys.

segments.title: Moving to New York: Ross, Charlie Skeet and Claude Hopkins
segments.summary: Hall goes to New York with Ross's band, plays a dancing school, then Charlie Skeet and Claude Hopkins at Roseland and the Savoy.

segments.title: Geechee Fields and Charlie Skeet's band lineup
segments.summary: Allen asks about trombonist Geechee Fields, and Hall describes Skeet's instrumentation and bassist Henry Turner.

segments.title: Gutty clarinet tone from the throat
segments.summary: Russell asks about Hall's strong tone; Hall says it just came naturally and comes from the throat, suiting blues more than ballads.

segments.title: Reeds, mouthpieces and the Albert system clarinet
segments.summary: Hall describes using medium reeds, only three mouthpieces in his life, and always playing the Albert system.

segments.title: Selma bought in Paris and borrowing a Buffet
segments.summary: Hall tells how he bought a Selma at the Paris factory during a European tour and borrowed a Buffet from Jimmy Dawson when it cracked.

segments.title: A clarinet on the Mutt Carey recordings
segments.summary: Hall used an A clarinet once, for the Mutt Carey Scott Joplin rag recordings, and never used C-sharp or E-flat instruments.

segments.title: Parade playing with Petit, Metcalf and Kelly
segments.summary: Hall played parades on a C clarinet with various bands, taking any advertising gig.

segments.title: Buddy Petit as inspiration and musician
segments.summary: Hall gives advice to young clarinetists and says Petit, who knew chords and read music, inspired him; discussion of Petit's derby mute and half-valves.

segments.title: Punch Miller, Jack Carey and riverboats
segments.summary: Hall recalls Lee Collins and Punch Miller with Jack Carey, never having cutting contests, and playing a riverboat only in St. Louis.

segments.title: Mutt Carey recordings and the Red Book
segments.summary: Hall met Mutt Carey in New York for their recordings, including African Misk; the group discusses reissues and the Red Books.

segments.title: Did bands use the Red Book; Petit's tone and ability
segments.summary: Hall says Petit read well, was the best trumpeter in his estimation, played mellow within the staff and seemed well schooled.

segments.title: Comparing Joe Oliver, Chris Kelly and Kid Rena to Petit
segments.summary: Hall compares Oliver, Chris Kelly, Kid Rena and Armstrong as players, saying Petit knew his instrument best.

segments.title: Jack Carey and Tiger Rag
segments.summary: Allen asks about unrecorded clarinetists, then Hall explains Jack Carey's fame for Tiger Rag, nicknamed for it.

segments.title: Brothers Robert, Edward, Clarence and Herbert
segments.summary: Hall describes his brothers' instruments and jobs, his singing sister, and a trumpet-playing uncle.

segments.title: Dewey relatives and Clarence still playing
segments.summary: Hall and Allen discuss relatives named Dewey and that brother Clarence still plays soprano.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet seen in New York and France
segments.summary: Hall speaks of soprano saxophonist Sidney Bechet, whom he met in New York after the war and visited in France.

segments.title: Where Hall's brothers played; wanting history of Petit
segments.summary: Hall's brothers played with Metcalf and Don Albert; Allen and Russell explain they want to document how Petit sounded.

segments.title: Petit as trumpet leader; Red Dugas; steady jobs
segments.summary: Hall calls Petit a leader other trumpeters followed, mentions drummer Red Dugas, and says steady jobs were rare, the first being Covington.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson, Picou and an unnamed Baton Rouge clarinetist
segments.summary: Hall says he did not know Bunk Johnson, comments on Picou, and describes a Baton Rouge clarinetist who played in any key with plugged keys.

segments.title: Father's Onward band trip to New York
segments.summary: Hall recounts meeting the last surviving Onward band tuba player, who described the New York festival the band won.

segments.title: Why Hall plays Albert system rather than Boehm
segments.summary: Hall tells how the Selma factory owner showed him Boehm clarinets dated 1853, and why he stays with Albert.

segments.title: Tone and speed on the Albert clarinet
segments.summary: Hall argues Albert clarinet has bigger tone for Dixieland; Allen praises Noone's tonguing; Hall's fast Clarinet Marmalade.

segments.title: Tempos in the old days and fingering differences
segments.summary: Hall says old bands never played fast, Tiger Rag the fastest, and he got faster with Teddy Wilson; he compares Albert and Boehm fingering.

segments.title: Two-beat versus four-beat and tuba versus string bass
segments.summary: Hall says New Orleans bands played two beat, and in New York dance bands used tuba, with Duke Hamilton's an exception.

segments.chapter: Rhythm sections, Rampart Street and church music
segments.title: Banjo, guitar and piano; Steve Lewis
segments.summary: Hall describes rhythm instruments in New Orleans bands, pianos at picnics and parades, and pianist Steve Lewis with Piron.

segments.chapter: Rhythm sections, Rampart Street and church music
segments.title: Tom Anderson's on Rampart Street and hearing Armstrong
segments.summary: Hall recalls Tom Anderson's cafe where he first heard Louis Armstrong with Zutty and a pianist.

segments.chapter: Rhythm sections, Rampart Street and church music
segments.title: Udell Wilson and Lil Hardin
segments.summary: Allen asks about pianist Udell Wilson, who worked with Armstrong, and Hall recalls only the name.

segments.chapter: Rhythm sections, Rampart Street and church music
segments.title: Church music and jazz; Hall's Catholic upbringing
segments.summary: Hall says sanctified church music is the root of rock and roll, and his family was Catholic.
